title: Mechanical Engineering
summary: Forces into structures, structures into machines. Bending (stress varies across a section) and resonance (a small push at the right frequency breaks big things) are the thresholds; the rest is learning to trust a model only as far as its assumptions.
sources: Hibbeler: Engineering Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics
Ashby: Materials Selection in Mechanical Design
Gordon: Structures, or Why Things Don't Fall Down

nodes.label: Statics & Equilibrium
nodes.summary: A body at rest has zero net force and zero net moment about every point.
nodes.outcome: Find support reactions of a loaded beam.
nodes.check: A 4 m beam on supports at each end carries 1000 N at its middle. What is each reaction?

nodes.label: Trusses & Frames
nodes.summary: Pin-jointed members carry only axial tension or compression; joints and sections solve them.
nodes.outcome: Find member forces by the method of joints.
nodes.check: Why do truss members carry only axial force?
nodes.answer: They are two-force members: pinned at both ends and loaded only at joints, so the force must lie along the member.

nodes.label: Stress & Strain
nodes.summary: Force per area (stress) and stretch per length (strain), linked by Young's modulus in the elastic range.
nodes.outcome: Compute the elongation of a loaded rod.
nodes.check: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa) carries 100 MPa of stress. What is its strain?

nodes.label: "Stiffer means stronger"
nodes.summary: Stiffness (modulus) measures resistance to deflection; strength measures the stress at failure. Glass is stiff and brittle; nylon is flexible and tough.
nodes.outcome: Distinguish stiffness, strength and toughness with examples.
nodes.check: Which is stiffer, aluminium or a typical steel, and is the stiffer one always stronger?
nodes.answer: Steel (~200 vs ~70 GPa); but a high-strength aluminium alloy can out-strengthen a mild steel. Stiffness is not strength.

nodes.label: Materials Selection
nodes.summary: Stiffness, strength, toughness, density and cost compared on Ashby charts to choose by performance index.
nodes.outcome: Choose a material for a light, stiff beam using a performance index.
nodes.check: For a light, stiff beam in bending, which index is maximised?
nodes.answer: E^(1/2) / ρ (Ashby's index for a beam of given stiffness and minimum mass).

nodes.label: Beam Bending
nodes.summary: Stress varies linearly across a bent section: tension on one face, compression on the other, zero at the neutral axis. Seeing this changes how every shape is judged.
nodes.outcome: Compute maximum bending stress with σ = My/I.
nodes.check: Why is a plank much stiffer on edge than flat?
nodes.answer: I = bh³/12 grows with the cube of the depth, so turning the plank on edge multiplies I.

nodes.label: "The middle of a beam carries the most"
nodes.summary: Bending stress is greatest at the outer fibres and zero at the neutral axis, which is why I-beams put material at the flanges.
nodes.outcome: Explain the shape of an I-beam from the stress distribution.
nodes.check: Where in a beam's cross-section is bending stress largest?
nodes.answer: At the top and bottom surfaces, farthest from the neutral axis.

nodes.label: Torsion & Shafts
nodes.summary: Twisting produces shear stress that grows with radius: τ = Tr/J.
nodes.outcome: Size a shaft to transmit a given power.
nodes.check: Why are drive shafts often hollow?
nodes.answer: Shear stress is greatest at the outside and the core carries little, so removing it saves much mass and little strength.

nodes.label: Buckling & Stability
nodes.summary: Slender columns fail by sideways instability at a load set by stiffness and length, not by strength (Euler).
nodes.outcome: Compute the Euler buckling load of a column.
nodes.check: If you double a column's length, what happens to its Euler buckling load?

nodes.label: Fatigue & Failure
nodes.summary: Repeated loads well below yield grow cracks; stress concentrations and endurance limits govern life.
nodes.outcome: Estimate fatigue life from an S–N curve and a stress concentration factor.
nodes.check: Why do aircraft windows have rounded corners?
nodes.answer: Sharp corners concentrate stress, starting fatigue cracks (the de Havilland Comet failures).

nodes.label: "It held the load once, so it's safe"
nodes.summary: A part can survive a load once and fail after a million cycles of a smaller one.
nodes.outcome: Explain why a static test does not prove fatigue life.
nodes.check: A paperclip doesn't break when bent once. Why does it break after bending back and forth?
nodes.answer: Each cycle grows tiny cracks (fatigue) until the remaining section fails.

nodes.label: Vibration & Resonance
nodes.summary: Every structure has natural frequencies; driving at one makes small forces produce large motion. Damping and detuning are the cures.
nodes.outcome: Compute a natural frequency and choose a design that avoids resonance.
nodes.check: A mass on a spring has a natural frequency of 10 Hz. A motor vibrates it at 10 Hz. What happens, and what are two fixes?
nodes.answer: Resonance (large amplitude). Change stiffness or mass to move the natural frequency, or add damping or isolation.

nodes.label: Mechanisms & Linkages
nodes.summary: Gears, cams and four-bar linkages turn one motion into another; degrees of freedom count what moves independently.
nodes.outcome: Compute a gear train ratio and a linkage's degrees of freedom.
nodes.check: A 20-tooth gear drives a 60-tooth gear. Output speed and torque compared with input?
nodes.answer: One third the speed and three times the torque (ignoring losses).

nodes.label: Thermodynamic Cycles
nodes.summary: Engines, refrigerators and power plants as cycles; Carnot sets the ceiling on efficiency.
nodes.outcome: Compute the Carnot efficiency between two temperatures.
nodes.check: What is the maximum efficiency of an engine running between 600 K and 300 K?

nodes.label: Fluid Mechanics
nodes.summary: Pressure, Bernoulli along a streamline, and the Reynolds number deciding laminar versus turbulent flow.
nodes.outcome: Predict laminar or turbulent flow from the Reynolds number.
nodes.check: What does a high Reynolds number indicate?
nodes.answer: Inertia dominates viscosity, so the flow tends to be turbulent.

nodes.label: Heat Transfer
nodes.summary: Conduction, convection and radiation, often modelled as thermal resistances in series.
nodes.outcome: Compute heat loss through a composite wall.
nodes.check: Why does a double-glazed window lose less heat than a single pane?
nodes.answer: The trapped gas layer adds a large thermal resistance in series.

nodes.label: Tolerances & Fits
nodes.summary: No part is exact; tolerances, fits and GD&T specify how much variation still works and assembles.
nodes.outcome: Choose a fit for a bearing on a shaft and stack up tolerances.
nodes.check: Why specify a tolerance at all instead of the exact size?
nodes.answer: Manufacturing always varies; the tolerance states what variation still works, and tighter costs more.

nodes.label: Design for Manufacturing
nodes.summary: Design so the part can actually be made, cheaply: draft angles, wall thickness, tool access, fewer parts.
nodes.outcome: Revise a part for injection moulding or 3D printing.
nodes.check: Why do injection-moulded parts have draft angles?
nodes.answer: So the part can be ejected from the mould without dragging and damage.

nodes.label: Finite Element Analysis
nodes.summary: Split a part into small elements, solve the stiffness equations, and check the answer against hand calculations.
nodes.outcome: Run an FEA, check mesh convergence and compare with a hand calculation.
nodes.check: Your FEA shows a stress 'hot spot' at a sharp re-entrant corner that grows with every mesh refinement. What is happening?
nodes.answer: A stress singularity: the ideal sharp corner has theoretically infinite stress. Add a real fillet radius or judge with a different criterion.

nodes.label: "The FEA colour plot is the truth"
nodes.summary: FEA is only as right as its loads, constraints, material data and mesh. Garbage in, colourful garbage out.
nodes.outcome: Validate an FEA with an independent hand estimate.
nodes.check: Name two independent checks before trusting an FEA result.
nodes.answer: A hand calculation (e.g. beam theory) of the same case, and a mesh-convergence study; also check reactions balance the applied loads.
